findings.claim: The whole-genome observation table has 12,311,588,080 rows (about 1.23e10): 153,894,851 variants times 80 populations, with one row for every population even where ac = 0. Rows cannot be dropped because a zero count over a known an is evidence, and silently dropping rows is forbidden.
findings.evidence: Koenig et al. 2024 report '153,894,851 high-quality variants across 4,094 individuals'. The repo adapter's docstring gives 80 populations. Arithmetic: 153,894,851 x 80 = 12,311,588,080.

findings.claim: In the design's own §2.5 format (all 17 OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA columns, zstd, 8,192-row groups, sorted by variant then population) the whole-genome table measures about 45-47 GB. Other layouts range from 9 GB to 197 GB: wide ac/an lists 9.1 GB; a 5-column slim table 14.2 GB; 122,880-row groups 30.9 GB; snappy (today's artifact format) 98.5 GB; population-major order 196.5 GB. source_record_id alone is 61% of the data bytes in the default layout, and leaving it out gives 20.6 GB.
findings.evidence: A synthetic 12M-row sample (4M rows for the sensitivity run), SEED 42. AN per population comes from the 73 real HGDP/1KG AN values the gnomAD API returned for chr11-5227002-T-A. Variant-id and rsid statistics come from a real 40 kb gnomAD v3 region (mean id length 17.8; 73% of variants carry an rsid). The run measured 3.676 B/row; with noisier AN and a rarer frequency spectrum it measured 3.806. Other layouts measured 0.74, 1.154, 2.511, 8.004 and 15.96 B/row. Each figure is scaled by 1.2312e10 rows. The default layout's footer is 0.245 B/row.

findings.claim: The raw whole-genome input in the adapter's TSV format (variant_id, rsid, pop_label, AC, AN) is about 52.6 GB zstd-compressed (62 GB gzip, 504 GB plain). The upstream gnomAD HGDP+1KG per-chromosome VCFs total 3,381.8 GiB (3.3 TiB), and gnomAD publishes an md5 for each.
findings.evidence: Measured on the 4M-row synthetic sample: 4.271 B/row zstd, 5.034 gzip, 40.941 plain. The upstream sizes are summed from gnomAD's GnomadV3Downloads.tsx list hgdpAnd1kgChromosomeVcfs (24 files).

findings.claim: Storing the table in GCS stays cheap: $0.86 a month at 46 GB, $1.86 at 100 GB, $3.73 at 200 GB, $9.31 at 500 GB and $37.25 at 2 TB. Table plus raw input (about 98 GB) is about $1.8 a month. Because releases are append-only, every re-ingest adds another full copy.
findings.evidence: Standard storage is $0.000027397 per GiB-hour, about $0.020 per GiB-month (the doc's $0.02/GiB), applied to each size in GiB.

findings.claim: Under the approved D1 (rule R3: tables/ is free at any size), a full bulk download from our bucket costs the user $0. It costs us $5.14 at 46 GB, $11.18 at 100 GB, $22.35 at 200 GB, $55.88 at 500 GB and $223.52 at 2 TB. Starting from zero spend, the $300 kill switch trips after about 58, 27, 13, 5 or 1.3 such downloads in a month. On top of the doc's 100x-users baseline ($186 a month from our bucket alone), it trips after 22 downloads at 46 GB, or half of one download at 2 TB.
findings.evidence: Egress is $0.12/GiB for 0-10 TiB (worldwide excluding Asia and Australia), $0.23 to China and $0.19 to Australia. The free tier is 100 GB a month from North America only. Calculation: size in GiB x $0.12, compared against $300.

findings.claim: Under the approved rule, the whole-genome release cannot ship from our bucket alone. Every measured layout (9 GB or more) is 4 to 900 times over the release guard, which caps a release's free bytes not held by a zero-egress mirror at 2 GiB, so the build fails unless a mirror holds the files, an owner override is made, or an owner PR raises the cap. Once published, rule R1 keeps the files free in our bucket permanently.
findings.evidence: Design §4.2: 'Release guard: open bytes on no zero-egress host, plus all R5 bytes, total <= 2 GiB per release, or the build fails'. R1: 'a path any earlier release published as open stays open and keeps gcs-free in hosts; CI fails if either shrinks'. Step 2.2 makes CI verify the HF copy before the manifest merges.

findings.claim: The kill switch reacts too slowly at this file size. Billing data lags by hours, and every 1 Gbit/s of whole-genome downloads costs about $50 an hour ($503 an hour at 10 Gbit/s). A few parallel clients could overshoot the $300 cap by hundreds of dollars before the bucket goes private, and when it does, every Atlas data download stops for everyone.
findings.evidence: 1 Gbit/s is 450 GB/h, which is 419 GiB/h; at $0.12/GiB that is $50/h. The design's §12 says the switch acts 'hours late because billing lags' and is all-or-nothing.

findings.claim: Querying only what is needed (the owner's principle) is cheap on our bucket. A one-variant lookup (80 rows) pulled 0.43 MB from a 5.9 MB file with 8,192-row groups, 3.03 MB from a 44 MB file (the 2.94 MB footer is 6.7% of the file), and 0.53 MB from a 30 MB file with 122,880-row groups. A 100 kb region (395,200 rows) pulled 1.2-4.3 MB. That is $0.05-0.34 per 1,000 lookups and $0.19-0.48 per 1,000 region queries.
findings.evidence: DuckDB 1.5.5 httpfs against a byte-logging Range server, with HTTP, file and parquet-metadata caches off. Point query: 6 GETs + 1 HEAD. Region: 126 GETs at 8,192-row groups, 14 at 122,880.

findings.claim: A genome-wide scan over HTTPS costs about as much as a bulk download. One population across every variant read 40% of the file's bytes; summing ac and an by population read 34% (25% with 122,880-row groups). From our bucket that is about $2.05 per scan at 46 GB, $8.92 at 200 GB and $89 at 2 TB. Such scans are impractical on the HF mirror without a token: about 1.5M GETs for a 46 GB table, which takes about 42 hours at HF's 3,000 anonymous requests per 5 minutes (4 hours with 122,880-row groups).
findings.evidence: Measured 17.6 of 44.1 MB and 15.2 of 44.1 MB, with 1,467 GETs per 44 MB file. HF's limit is the design's own [hf-rate] citation.

findings.claim: A BigQuery copy of the whole-genome table holds 2,642 GiB (2.58 TiB) of logical data. Our storage would cost $52.6 a month for the first 90 days and $26.3 a month after on logical billing. On compressed ('physical') billing it is roughly $1-7 a month, but only if BigQuery compresses like Parquet, which is unmeasured. D6a's 'under $5 a month' holds only on compressed billing. Leaving out source_record_id saves 19%.
findings.evidence: Measured BigQuery logical bytes on the synthetic rows: 230.46 B/row (STRING = 2 + UTF-8 bytes, INT64/FLOAT64 = 8, BOOL = 1); source_record_id alone is 42.9 B/row. US multi-region prices parsed from Google's saved pricing-page data: active logical $0.02, long-term logical $0.01, active physical $0.04, long-term physical $0.02 per GiB-month; the first 10 GiB is free. Batch loads are free in the shared slot pool; cross-region loads are billed.
findings.source: factcheck-dl/bigquery_pricing.html (embedded per-region data; 'US (us)' table); factcheck-dl/bigquery_pricing.txt lines 82-90, 488-498, 856, 1544

findings.claim: Querying the BigQuery copy costs the querier, never us. A SELECT * over the whole genome reads 2.58 TiB: $9.88 if it fits the querier's monthly free 1 TiB first, $16.13 if not. A scan of only variant_id, population_id, ac and an reads 0.543 TiB, which is free within the 1 TiB and $3.39 beyond it. At Google's 10 MB minimum per table per query, the free 1 TiB covers about 105,000 point lookups a month per billing account; the bytes clustering actually prunes to are unmeasured.
findings.evidence: $6.25/TiB on-demand after the first 1 TiB a month. 'The data owner is not charged when their data is accessed.' 'minimum 10 MB data processed per table referenced'.

findings.claim: Bounded queries stay cheap; bulk downloads and genome-wide scans set the bill. Assumed 100x month: 400,000 lookups, 20,000 regions, 500 scans, 500 whole-genome pulls. If everything comes from our bucket, list price is $3.6k at 46 GB and $156k at 2 TB, so the kill switch fires within days. If a mirror carries 90% of pulls and BigQuery takes the scans, it is $269 at 46 GB and $11k at 2 TB, because the 10% of pulls that fall back to our bucket dominates. If whole-genome pulls never fall back to our bucket and scans go to BigQuery, only about $12 of bounded-query egress remains after the free tier ($23 if the doc's baseline has already used the free tier).
findings.evidence: Decomposition at 46 GB, 100x: queries 193 GiB, scans 8,552 GiB, downloads 21,420 GiB. The traffic figures are assumptions in the style of the doc's planning model: the doc's 50 full downloads now times 10% that include whole genome, times 100; about 2 lookups per Atlas visit.

findings.claim: With the recommended setup, the 100x month with whole genome comes to about $94-166, still under the $200 budget. That is the doc's $68 (100x users and data, HF copy first) plus about $23 of bounded-query egress, about $2 of GCS storage, $1-7 for BigQuery on compressed billing ($26-53 on logical) and $0-20 for an HF plan. The setup is: mirror-only bulk, BigQuery for scans, small files.
findings.evidence: Sum of the findings above, plus the HF Team price of $20 per user per month.

findings.claim: Small files and file-listing views trade query egress against index size. Each part URL a catalog view lists adds about 470 B to the views-only DuckDB catalog: 920 files give 0.54 MB, 7,667 files give 3.7 MB, against 274 KB today. The doc measured an attach reading 2x the file, so a 7,667-file catalog would cost about 7 MB per session, $0.83 per 1,000 sessions, more than 1,000 point lookups ($0.05). The manifest grows at 429 B per object: 7,667 parts (6 MB files) give 3.3 MB, which crosses D14's 2 MB trigger at the first whole-genome release; 920 parts (50 MB files) give 0.4 MB.
findings.evidence: Measured catalog files of 536,576 B and 3,682,304 B with production-length URLs. The 2026-10-18 manifest is 106,409 B for 248 objects. The design measured 548,868 B read for a 274,432 B attach.

findings.claim: The website cannot serve whole-genome observations as one web JSON file per variant. Writing 153,894,851 objects costs about $769 in upload operations per publish, so the website's whole-genome observations layer has to read the data store by range query (about 0.43 MB per variant measured) or through the planned P4 lookup API. That traffic then falls under the data bucket's kill switch.
findings.evidence: Standard Class A operations cost $0.005 per 1,000: 153,894,851 / 1,000 x $0.005 = $769.

findings.claim: A free Hugging Face organisation does not guarantee whole-genome scale. Public storage on a free account is 'Best-effort', and beyond 'the first few gigabytes' substantial storage needs PRO, Team or Enterprise. PRO is $9 a month with up to 10 TB public; Team is $20 per user per month with 12 TB base plus 1 TB per seat; extra public storage is $12/TB-month. HF recommends under 100k files per repo, under 10k per folder and files under 200 GB (500 GB hard). Fallbacks: R2 at $0.015/GB-month with no egress fees ($0.69 at 46 GB, $4.5 at 300 GB, $30 at 2 TB). AWS Open Data covers 'storing and sharing' openly licensed data and says it decides 'generally within a two-week period'. Google's Public Dataset Program pays storage (contact bq-public-data@google.com).
findings.evidence: Quoted from the pages fetched 2026-10-19; Google's program text from the saved access-web/bq_public.txt.

findings.claim: gnomAD's primary data is CC0, so the whole-genome table can go on the Google-billed doors (D2c) and to AWS Open Data. This holds if its inputs are only the gnomAD AC/AN harvest and the HGDP/1KG registry rows (now CC BY 4.0 under D5a). Because a derived object carries the union of its inputs' sources, feeding it the whole P0 registry would pull in AFND and other sources. gnomAD also asks users not to re-identify participants, and some annotations are non-commercial (SpliceAI is CC BY-NC), so the harvest should carry only counts.
findings.evidence: gnomAD terms: 'The primary data from the gnomAD exomes and genomes are available free of restrictions under the Creative Commons Zero Public Domain Dedication'; 'All users of gnomAD data agree to not attempt to reidentify participants'; 'SpliceAI ... CC BY NC 4.0'. Design §4.2: 'a derived object's sources are the computed union of its inputs' sources'.

findings.claim: The current ingest code cannot run at whole-genome scale. The adapter reads the whole TSV with pandas and validates it with pandera, including a uniqueness check on source_record_id over the full table. At 1.23e10 rows (2.8 TB logical) it must work one chromosome or bin at a time and check uniqueness out of memory. One chromosome (chr1 is about 8% of the genome) is about 4 GB raw plus 3.6 GB table, which fits a free runner's 14 GB disk. Each ingest means an owner upload of about 100 GB (table plus raw), or about 300 GB with a population-major copy.
findings.evidence: gnomad_hgdp_1kg.py: pd.read_csv(path) then OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA.validate(obs); schema.py: source_record_id unique=True. Per-chromosome sizes scale the measured totals.

research: costs.implications:
I measured local synthetic data shaped by real HGDP/1KG allele counts. In the design's own §2.5 format, the whole-genome observation table comes to about 45-47 GB, not 100 GB-2 TB. Other layouts span 9 GB (wide ac/an lists) to 197 GB (population-major order). The raw input adds about 53 GB. All costs below are given for 46, 100, 200, 500 GB and 2 TB, so the layout angle's final size can be plugged in. Every row stores integer ac and an, never ac/an; observations and surfaces stay separate (D4 widens observations only; surfaces stay at the fitted variants).

WHAT THE APPROVED FREE RULE (D1) MEANS AT THIS SIZE
- A full download is free to the user. From our bucket it costs us $5.14 at 46 GB and $223.52 at 2 TB.
- The $300 kill switch trips after about 58 such downloads in a month at 46 GB, or 1.3 at 2 TB. With the doc's 100x-users baseline already spent, it trips after 22 downloads at 46 GB, or half of one at 2 TB.
- The release guard (2 GiB a release not held by a mirror) fails any whole-genome build unless a mirror holds the files. So the mirror is a precondition, not just a saving.
- Rule R1 then keeps the files free in our bucket permanently.
- The kill switch acts hours late. Each Gbit/s of downloads costs about $50 an hour, and when the switch fires, every Atlas data download stops for everyone.

QUERY-FIRST AND COSTS AGREE
- Querying only what is needed is cheap: a variant lookup reads 0.43 MB (small files), a 100 kb region 1.2-1.7 MB.
- At an assumed 100x traffic, bounded queries cost about $12-23 a month.
- Only bulk downloads and genome-wide scans move the whole table. A genome-wide scan reads about 40% of it: $2 at 46 GB, $89 at 2 TB. Those two must leave our bucket.
- With mirror-only bulk downloads and BigQuery for scans, the 100x month is about $94-166, still under $200. Served only from our bucket, it is thousands of dollars at list price, which means the kill switch would fire every month.

DECISIONS THAT CHANGE STATUS
- D2a, D2c and D6a move from later to now, because step 3.1 (BigQuery) starts with D4 = whole genome.
- D6a's 'under $5 a month' no longer holds on logical billing ($26-53 a month). It holds only on compressed ('physical') billing, estimated at $1-7 a month (unmeasured until load).
- D3 becomes a precondition for the first whole-genome release.
- D3b is superseded by the builder's call: no implicit default. fetch_data.py's `--set tables` and offline mode must exclude whole-genome parts, which are 45 GB or more.
- D12a moves earlier: apply before the release. AWS decides in about two weeks. Google's Public Dataset Program is added in parallel. D12b is not needed for this table if its inputs exclude AFND and MAP.
- D14 likely fires at the first whole-genome release if files are about 6 MB: about 7,700 objects make a 3.3 MB manifest.
- D7, D10, D11 and D13 keep their timing but matter more. D11: whole-genome observations can't be one web JSON file per variant (about $769 of upload operations per publish). D13: the HF ask should cover whole genome plus draws (about 150-500 GB).
- D8 and D9 stay untriggered if the raw input is cut into parts of 1 GiB or less (each part stays free under R4).
- D2b and D15: unchanged, confirm only.

REFRAMED AND NEW QUESTIONS, EACH WITH A RECOMMENDATION
- D3 (reframed): Querying stays the main path: from our bucket, free, about 0.4 MB per variant. Bulk downloads (45-200 GB) and genome-wide scans move the whole table. Should they come from a free mirror, with fetch_data.py never falling back to our bucket for whole-genome files unless asked, and printing the cost when asked?
  We recommend: yes. Start with an HF organisation dataset (ask HF for a storage grant; otherwise Team at $20 a month for 13 TB). Apply to AWS Open Data and Google's program in parallel. R2 is the paid fallback ($1-5 a month at 100-300 GB).
- D2a (reframed): Genome-wide SQL scans go to BigQuery or to a downloaded copy, not to anonymous HTTPS. In BigQuery the querier pays; a scan of variant_id, population_id, ac and an fits the querier's free 1 TiB a month, and SELECT * costs $10-16. Accept that a genome-wide scan needs a Google account or a download?
  We recommend: yes. The catalog's whole-genome queries require a variant or region.
- D2c: Does a door where Google bills the user count as charging?
  We recommend: yes, unchanged. The table qualifies once gnomAD's CC0 terms entry (step 1.8) and the D5a/D5b evidence are recorded, and its inputs are only the gnomAD harvest plus the HGDP/1KG registry rows.
- D6a: Create the BigQuery project now?
  We recommend: yes, with compressed ('physical') storage billing and its own budget. Ask Google's Public Dataset Program to host the copy, which would make our storage cost $0.
- D12a (moved earlier): Open the AWS account now and apply to AWS Open Data and Google's program for this table only?
  We recommend: yes.
- D16 (new): Serve whole-genome files from their own bucket, in a project with its own budget and kill switch, so a stampede on them doesn't make all Atlas data private?
  We recommend: yes. R1 makes the free copy permanent, and the switch is all-or-nothing and late.
- D17 (new): Publish our extracted per-population counts (about 53 GB zstd, in parts of 1 GiB or less) as the raw input, and cite gnomAD's 3.3 TiB VCFs by URL and md5 instead of re-hosting them?
  We recommend: yes. This keeps the raw input free and the paid tiers untriggered.
- Guard: keep the 2 GiB cap? We recommend: yes. A release waits for its mirror rather than raising the cap.

THE OWNER'S HANDS-ON STEPS GROW
- Each ingest means uploading about 100-300 GB.
- The adapter must run one chromosome at a time; whole-file pandas validation cannot run at 1.23e10 rows.

DISCLOSURE
One measurement step accidentally made a single anonymous HTTPS GET to a path in the production data bucket that does not exist (DuckDB was binding a view, and it got a 404). No cloud command or credential was used, and later measurements used a local server.

Scratch work is in <scratchpad>/wg/costs-tiers/ (scripts/gen_measure.py, scripts/query_bytes.py, scripts/costs.py, out/costs.txt). The disk had only about 2.5 GB free, so the sample files were kept small.

findings.claim: For v1's whole-genome observations layer, the only open source of per-population allele counts that is whole-genome, GRCh38 and placeable on a map is gnomAD's HGDP+1KG subset. It covers 80 populations (54 HGDP + 26 1KG). No other source checked combines all three, so it should be the primary source.
findings.evidence: Koenig et al. 2024: "we harmonized a high-quality set of 4094 whole genomes from 80 populations"; Results/Methods give 153,894,851 SNVs and indels. Every other source checked (findings below) fails one of the three. 1000G-HC and HGDP-Bergström publish no per-population counts and are already inside this subset. ALFA groups are ancestry groups, not places. IndiGen is a single all-India aggregate. AADR and SGDP are hg19. MCPS and GenomeIndia cannot be redistributed.

findings.claim: gnomAD's terms allow us to redistribute derived per-population counts and to charge for them, including cost recovery. Two binding conditions remain: no re-identification, and a trademark request.
findings.evidence: terms.md: "The primary data from the gnomAD exomes and genomes are available free of restrictions under the Creative Commons Zero Public Domain Dedication. This means that you can use it for any purpose without legally having to give attribution." Also: "All users of gnomAD data agree to not attempt to reidentify participants." Also: "Some annotations may have restrictions on usage. For instance, SpliceAI annotations ... CC BY NC 4.0". The trademark request: "refrain from incorporating 'gnomAD' or 'Genome Aggregation Database' into the name of your tool". The repo already records gnomAD as explicitly_open (docs/audits/gnomad-dbsnp-commercial-use.md). Per-population AC/AN are primary frequency data, not annotations.

findings.claim: In the v3.1.2 HGDP+1KG dense VCF, the per-population counts carry only 78 population labels, not 80. Han+NorthernHan and PapuanHighlands+PapuanSepik are merged, so these counts cannot fill the registry's 80 identities without recounting from genotypes.
findings.evidence: Measured: the chr22 header (read remotely with bcftools) has 1,174 INFO fields and 4,151 sample columns. AC_<pop> fields without the _XX/_XY suffix give 78 labels, including 'han' and 'papuan' but no northernhan or papuanhighlands. This matches the repo's pilot finding of 78 display labels against 80 literal source populations. Files: 24 per-chromosome VCFs totalling 3,381.84 GiB per the download-page source (chr22 59,465,212,964 B).

findings.claim: The dense VCF's per-population counts cover only the ~3,380 unrelated high-quality samples, not the 4,094-person cohort.
findings.evidence: Measured on chr22:20,000,001-20,010,000 (616 records) and chr11:5,200,001-5,250,000 (3,812 records). The 78 per-population AN values sum exactly to INFO AN at every site (max difference 0), and per-population AC sums equal AC at 616/616 and 3,812/3,812 sites. Median INFO AN is 6,760 (3,380 diploid samples). Documented definition: hgdp_tgp_freq is "Allele frequency information ... in HGDP + 1KG samples that pass the high_quality sample annotation and are inferred as unrelated".

findings.claim: No gnomAD sites VCF contains HGDP or 1KG population counts. The v3.1.2 genomes sites VCF (2,333.03 GiB) and the v4.1.1 genomes sites VCF carry only gnomAD's broad genetic ancestry groups, and gnomAD's export code drops the hgdp and tgp fields on purpose.
findings.evidence: Measured headers. v3.1.2 sites chr22 subsets are afr, ami, amr, asj, eas, fin, mid, nfe, oth, sas plus the non_cancer/non_neuro/non_topmed/non_v2/controls subsets; there are no hgdp or tgp fields. This contradicts the downloads page sentence "contain all subsets (... 1KG, and HGDP)". v4.1.1 genomes chr22 groups are afr, ami, amr, asj, eas, fin, grpmax, mid, nfe, remaining, sas. gnomad_qc v4 validate_and_export_vcf.py: "# Drop any info annotation with \"hgdp\" or \"tgp\" in the name for genomes."

findings.claim: In bulk, gnomAD's 80-population v4 counts exist only in Hail tables, which need Hail/Spark to read. Three bulk routes exist, at very different sizes.
findings.evidence: Sizes were measured from anonymous GCS listings; row counts come from the metadata.json.gz partition counts. (a) v4.1 genomes sites HT: 759,336,320 rows, 565.20 GiB; the browser pipeline reads its hgdp and tgp subsets. (b) v3.1.2 hgdp_1kg_subset_variant_annotations HT: 207,270,207 rows (every site, filtered ones included), 225.72 GiB, carrying hgdp_tgp_freq. (c) Dense VCF: 3,381.84 GiB, readable with bcftools; it is the only route that can recount the 4,094-person cohort under 80 identities, as the repo's chr22 pilot did.

findings.claim: gnomAD publishes three different sets of HGDP+1KG counts for the same variant. The ingest must pin one release and sample set in cohort_id and ingest_version. The current adapter's labels do not agree with each other.
findings.evidence: Measured for rs334 (chr11-5227002-T-A). Dense v3.1.2 VCF: 78 labels, sum AC 161, sum AN 6,754. gnomAD API v3 (gnomad_r3): 73 labels, AC 149, AN 6,554; five HGDP populations are absent (biaka, mbuti, melanesian, papuan, san); 21 of 78 labels identical. gnomAD API v4 (gnomad_r4): 80 labels, including northernhan, papuanhighlands and papuansepik; AC 160, AN 6,672; 50 of 78 identical. Example: hgdp:han AN is 86 dense, 84 in v3, and 66 (+20 northernhan) in v4. genomeos/observations/sources/gnomad_hgdp_1kg.py sets COHORT_ID 'gnomad-v4-hgdp-1kg', but its docstring describes '4,094 genomes', and no published gnomAD count set is drawn from those 4,094.

findings.claim: A whole-genome HGDP+1KG observations table has about 1.23e10 rows (1.62e10 if non-PASS sites are kept). As long-format zstd Parquet it would take about 8.7 GB with 4 columns, about 17 GB with the full schema minus a stored source_record_id, and about 65 GB with all 17 OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA columns.
findings.evidence: Row counts: 153,894,851 × 80 = 12,311,588,080 rows; 207,270,207 × 78 = 1.62e10. Measured bytes per row (zstd, 8,192-row groups, sorted by variant_id) on 48,048 and 297,336 real rows: 0.71 B/row for (variant_id, population, ac, an); 1.34–1.42 B/row for 16 columns without source_record_id; 5.23–5.28 B/row for all 17 columns, where the unique source_record_id string alone costs about 3.8 B/row. Extrapolating to the genome is an inference from two blocks totalling 4,428 sites.

findings.claim: Most cells are zero counts and must still be stored, because an carries the evidence. Some cells have an = 0, which OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA rejects, so the ingest needs a counted refusal reason for them rather than a silent drop.
findings.evidence: Measured: 91.7% (chr22) and 89.2% (chr11) of (variant, population) cells have ac = 0. Cells with an = 0: 5 of 48,048 (chr22) and 616 of 297,336 (chr11, at 143 of 3,812 sites). The schema declares an as pa.Check.gt(0). Also, 41 of the 616 chr22 records are non-PASS (AC0, AS_VQSR), so the FILTER policy must be explicit. All 4,428 sampled records have REF/ALT matching [ACGT]+ (632 are indels).

findings.claim: The phased HGDP+1KG haplotypes and the phased 1000G high-coverage panel are small (18.72 GiB and 30.0 GiB), but neither is a valid observation source. Phasing fills in missing genotypes and singletons were removed, so counts derived from them are partly inferred, which would mix inferred values into observations.
findings.evidence: Measured on chr22:20,000,001-20,010,000. HGDP+1KG phased_haplotypes_v2 (4,091 samples): 302 records, AN = 8,182 on every record, no genotype missing, no AC < 2. Its header records 'bcftools view -iMAC>=2' and 'shapeit5 phase_rare'. In the same interval the dense VCF has 616 records, and the repo pilot counted 15,565 missing genotypes. 1000G HC phased panel: 271 records, AN = 6,404 (3,202 × 2) on every record, no AC < 2.

findings.claim: gnomAD's HGDP+1KG files can be read anonymously and for free from both Google Cloud Storage and AWS Open Data. That contradicts the paper's 'requester-pays' wording for this bucket.
findings.evidence: Measured with anonymous HEAD requests: chr22 hgdp_tgp VCF is 59,465,212,964 B on storage.googleapis.com (gcp-public-data--gnomad; md5 eb04c341491a1553cb020bb0d2a4cf36, identical to the download page) and on gnomad-public-us-east-1.s3.amazonaws.com. The AWS registry lists License: "MIT; terms of use" and "No AWS account required". Koenig et al. say "publicly available in requester-pays Google Cloud Platform buckets". The Azure mirror host did not resolve.

findings.claim: The 1000 Genomes high-coverage data (3,202 samples, GRCh38) publishes counts only for its 5 superpopulations, not its 26 populations. Its terms grant no licence. It also must not be ingested separately, because 3,199 of its 3,202 samples are already in the gnomAD subset.
findings.evidence: Measured: the phased-panel and raw-GT headers have AC/AN only for EAS, AMR, EUR, AFR and SAS (plus _unrel). Sizes: phased panel 30.0 GiB (23 files); raw GT 1,641.9 GiB (25 files). Sample-ID overlap with the gnomAD dense VCF: 3,199 of 3,202. IGSR disclaimer: "Data from the 1000 Genomes Project is now available without embargo"; "restrictions on different pieces of data within IGSR and rights claimed on pieces of data vary"; "It remains the responsibility of users to ensure that their exploitation of the data" does not infringe third-party rights. IGSR FAQ: "The 1000 Genomes data is made available according to the Fort Lauderdale Agreement." Charging is not addressed.

findings.claim: HGDP from Bergström et al. 2020 (929 genomes, GRCh38) likewise publishes no per-population counts and overlaps the gnomAD subset. Its data terms are open without a licence; the CEPH academic-only condition applies to DNA samples, not to data.
findings.evidence: Measured: 24 VCFs, about 317.1 GiB, at ngs.sanger.ac.uk/production/hgdp/hgdp_wgs.20190516/; INFO has only overall AC/AN; 929 samples. 802 of 929 IDs exactly match the gnomAD subset, which also holds 121 IDs that are not HGDP-, HG- or NA-prefixed, such as LP6005441-DNA_*. README.data-access: "This data is freely available with no restrictions on the types of analyses that can be carried out." IGSR README_HGDP_datareuse_statement: "Please observe the Fort Lauderdale principles". CEPH: "Collaborators must agree to use the DNA samples for academic research only". Charging is not addressed.

findings.claim: NCBI ALFA offers bulk per-population counts on GRCh38, but its 12 populations are ancestry groups, not sampling places, so they cannot get the coordinate and radius the registry requires. Link to ALFA; do not ingest it as observations. Its terms also forbid re-identifying groups.
findings.evidence: Measured: freq.vcf.gz is 18G (release build_id 20260205170148), with FORMAT AN:AC per BioSample column (12 columns), RefSeq contigs and multi-allelic records (rs334 T>A,C,G; e.g. SAMN10492705=74190:136,0,2). Docs: "12 diverse populations" and an API at api.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/variation/v0/. The GSR terms of use say users "Will not attempt to re-identify or contact any individual or group within a study population" and "Will promote scientific research or health". Neither redistribution nor charging is addressed.

findings.claim: The gnomAD API can link a single variant to its 80 HGDP+1KG population counts, but it cannot supply the whole genome. It is rate-limited, and it omits the zero-count populations whenever the whole subset lacks the allele.
findings.evidence: Code (gnomad-v4-variant-queries.ts): "if (variant.genome.freq.hgdp.ac_raw > 0) { ... id: `hgdp:${pop.id}`", and the same for tgp. So when the subset-wide raw AC is 0, the populations, including their AN, are not returned. A community report, not gnomAD policy, describes "the API request limit of 10 requests per minute" and a batch limit of 25. At 25 variants per request and 10 requests per minute, 153.9M variants would take about 427 days (inference).

findings.claim: Ensembl's REST API already serves 1000 Genomes phase 3 counts for its 26 populations, mapped to GRCh38, per variant. It can be linked rather than rebuilt.
findings.evidence: Measured: /variation/human/rs334?pops=1 returned 115 population rows with keys allele, allele_count, frequency and population. For example, 1000GENOMES:phase_3:GWD has A=26 and T=200; the mapping assembly is GRCh38. The documented limit is "55000 requests over an hour" ("an average of 15 requests per second").

findings.claim: The Geography of Genetic Variants (GGV) browser serves counts with coordinates, but only on hg19, its API is undocumented, and its HGDP dataset is switched off. Link to it; do not depend on it.
findings.evidence: Measured: vis.js lists datasets 1000genomes, 1000genomes_superpops, ExAC and POPRES_Euro, all build 'hg19'; the 'HGDPimputedto1000genomes' entry is commented out. The API ggv_api/freq_table?data="1000genomes_table"&rsID=rs334 returned 26 populations with nobs/xobs counts and lat/lon (GWD nobs 226, xobs 26, at 11:5248232, i.e. GRCh37). The footer has a CC BY 4.0 link with no accompanying text.

findings.claim: PGG.SNV is browser-only: it states no terms or licence and offers no bulk download. It stays an outreach request, as v1 §14.3 says, and is linked meanwhile.
findings.evidence: User guide: "It now documents 71,080,900 human SNVs distribute on 200,000 human genomes representing 500 global populations" (the 2019 paper said 265M SNVs and 977 populations). The default build shown is GRCh37, with a separate GRCh38 site. The footer reads only "Copyright©2017". Only per-table CSV/TXT/XLS/SQL export buttons exist.

findings.claim: The MCPS licence forbids redistributing, selling, sublicensing or crawling its data, so MCPS can only be linked.
findings.evidence: Licence text extracted from the site's JS bundle: "a limited, revocable, royalty-free, non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-sublicensable, license"; "Any unauthorized transfer or use ... (including any sale of the Data to any third party), automatically terminates". Users may not "copy or use the Website or the Content in any manner except as expressly permitted", may not "directly sell, lease, license or transfer the Website or the Content for monetary or other commercial gain", and may not "use software robots, spiders, crawlers". The licence also says "ALL DATA IS FOR RESEARCH PURPOSES ONLY".

findings.claim: GenomeAsia 100K (GAsP) says its population-specific counts are freely downloadable, but its site was unreachable on 2026-10-19 and no licence or genome build has been verified. Until then its terms are not_checked.
findings.evidence: Nature 2019 data statement: "summary data for genotype quality, allele depth and population-specific allele counts were calculated" and "This dataset is available without requirement for login or other form of restriction for browsing or for download at https://browser.genomeasia100k.org." Individual-level data go through administrative review, and Malaysian samples carry extra restrictions. Measured: browser.genomeasia100k.org and genomeasia100k.org timed out after 30 s.

findings.claim: IndiGen publishes no per-population counts (one all-India aggregate), restricts use to academic work, and offers a download of only its unique variants. GenomeIndia is controlled-access. Neither can feed the public whole-genome layer.
findings.evidence: IndiGen (NAR 2021): "is made freely available for academic utility"; 1,029 genomes; 55,898,122 variants on GRCh38. The interface shows overall allele count, number and frequency, and "The VCF file containing variants unique to IndiGenomes has been made available for download." GenomeIndia (10,074 genomes, 83 populations) is under managed access at IBDC via the FeED protocols, according to press and secondary sources; the primary terms were not read.

findings.claim: AADR and SGDP are not whole-genome GRCh38 count sources. AADR is CC0 but covers a fixed SNP panel on hg19; SGDP is hg19 with 1–3 samples per population and partly signed-letter access.
findings.evidence: Measured via the Dataverse API: AADR v66.p1 (released 2026-06-08) has licence "CC0 1.0", 25 files, 33,038,215,366 B, and the description says "genotyped at up to an expanded set of 2 million positions in the genome (in hg19 coordinates)". SGDP: the Reich lab page lists 300 samples from 142 populations, with 21 signed-letter VCFs available on request; the Simons Foundation asks users to observe Fort Lauderdale.

findings.claim: The sources already ingested do not change this picture. WBBC gives regional AF and AN only, with AC reconstructed and no stated licence. AFND (HLA/KIR) and MAP (HbS/G6PD) are not whole-genome.
findings.evidence: From the repo. wbbc.py: "reports AF and AN ... but no regional AC"; assay 'genome_frequency_reconstructed'. The WBBC research note says "states no processed-data licence and no explicit redistribution or commercial-use restriction", which the repo records as no_restriction_found. The afnd_* and map_* adapters cover HLA/KIR/cytokine loci and HbS/G6PD only.

findings.claim: The current gnomAD adapter cannot run at whole-genome scale. It needs a chunked writer that validates each partition and builds IDs deterministically.
findings.evidence: gnomad_hgdp_1kg.load does pd.read_csv on a whole TSV, then OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA.validate, which checks source_record_id for uniqueness across the whole frame. Even at the measured 5.25 B/row in compressed Parquet, 1.23e10 rows is about 65 GB compressed, and far more in memory. wbbc.py already scans in pandas chunks.

findings.claim: A 17–65 GB whole-genome table collides with the platform design's 2 GiB-per-release guard on bytes no mirror holds. Looking up one variant stays cheap, which fits the owner's query-first principle.
findings.evidence: Platform design §4.2: R3 makes `tables/` free at any size, but "open bytes on no zero-egress host ... total ≤ 2 GiB per release, or the build fails". So the table needs the Hugging Face mirror (the reframed D3) or an owner PR that raises the guard. A full pull costs $1.9–7.3 at $0.12/GiB. Inference: if sorted by variant with 8,192-row groups, one variant's 80 rows fall in about one row group, about 43 KB at 5.25 B/row plus the footer. gnomAD's CC0 is explicitly_open, so the D2c terms gate would admit this table to BigQuery; the platform design starts BigQuery (step 3.1) when D4 = whole genome.

research: sources.implications:
With D4 = whole genome and query-first adopted, the plan for v1's observations layer is to derive one source in bulk, gnomAD's HGDP+1KG subset, and to link everything else.

1. **Primary source.** HGDP+1KG is CC0 (explicitly_open), so we may redistribute it and charge for it. It is GRCh38, has 80 populations that can be placed on the map (the registry supplies coordinates and radii), and can be read anonymously on GCS and AWS at no cost to us. No other open source checked is all three of whole-genome, GRCh38 and placeable.
   - 1000G high coverage and HGDP Bergström are already inside it: 3,199 of 3,202 and 802 of 929 sample IDs match. Ingesting either separately would count the same people twice.
   - SGDP, AADR and PGG.SNV are hg19/GRCh37 or browser-only. IndiGen is an all-India aggregate for academic use only. GenomeIndia is controlled-access. MCPS's licence forbids redistribution and crawling. ALFA's 12 groups are ancestries, not places, so they cannot get a coordinate and radius; adding them as observations would be a hard error.

2. **The owner must choose which gnomAD counts.** gnomAD publishes three different sets, and they disagree (rs334: 21 to 50 of 78 labels identical):
   - **v3.1.2 dense VCF INFO:** 78 labels with Han and Papuan merged, unrelated high-quality samples only (~3,380). It does not fit the registry's 80 identities.
   - **v4.1 sites Hail table:** 80 labels, gnomAD's v4 sample set. 565 GiB, Hail only.
   - **Recount from genotypes** in the 3.38 TiB dense VCF for the 4,094-person cohort (or another sample set we define), under 80 identities. This is the method the repo already proved on chr22.

   The phased panels must not be used: missing genotypes are filled by phasing and singletons are dropped. That would put inferred values into observations.

   The choice must be recorded in cohort_id and ingest_version. The adapter's COHORT_ID 'gnomad-v4-hgdp-1kg' and its '4,094 genomes' docstring describe different count sets, which needs fixing.

3. **Scale.**
   - About 1.23e10 rows; 89–92% of cells are ac = 0 and must be kept, because an carries the evidence.
   - About 0.01–0.2% of cells have an = 0. The schema rejects these, so they need a counted refusal reason.
   - Measured Parquet extrapolates to about 17 GB if source_record_id is derived rather than stored, about 65 GB if stored, and about 8.7 GB for the 4 core columns.
   - The current adapter (pandas plus a frame-wide uniqueness check) cannot run at this scale. It needs a chunked writer that validates each partition.
   - The table exceeds the platform design's 2 GiB guard on bytes no mirror holds. That makes the Hugging Face mirror (re-asked D3) or a guard-raising PR a precondition. The table should be sorted and partitioned so that looking up one variant reads only about one row group.

4. **Link rather than rebuild.**
   - gnomAD browser and API: 80 v4 populations per variant. It is rate-limited and drops zero-count populations when the subset lacks the allele, so it cannot stand in for the bulk table.
   - Ensembl REST: 1000G phase 3, 26 populations, GRCh38 counts.
   - GGV: hg19 counts with coordinates; undocumented API.
   - ALFA: 12 ancestry groups, bulk VCF plus API.
   - PGG.SNV, MCPS, GenomeAsia and IndiGen browsers.

   What genomeOS adds is the registry join (coordinates, radius, ascertainment fields). No upstream publishes that.

5. **Terms to record by evidence PR.**
   - gnomAD is already explicitly_open.
   - 1000G/IGSR and HGDP-Sanger: no_restriction_found (Fort Lauderdale; no licence; charging not addressed).
   - ALFA: no_restriction_found, with the GSR clause against re-identifying any individual or group.
   - MCPS: restricted (link only).
   - IndiGen: academic only.
   - GenomeAsia: not_checked (site unreachable 2026-10-19).
   - AADR: CC0.
   - None of this reopens #66.

findings.claim: The measurements use real gnomAD data: 102,594 polymorphic PASS variants from chr21:25,000,001-27,000,000 turn into 7,974,942 rows that match the 17-column observations contract. Every row passes the repo's own observations schema.
findings.evidence: bcftools 1.21 streamed the region over anonymous HTTPS (no gcloud) from gnomad.genomes.v3.1.2.hgdp_tgp.chr21.vcf.bgz (55,039,425,858 B, generation 1635563729562208). It returned 120,579 records: 106,849 PASS, and 102,594 PASS with subset AC>0. The VCF has 78 per-population AC_/AN_ fields. Rows follow the conventions of genomeos/observations/sources/gnomad_hgdp_1kg.py: source_record_id is 'gnomad-hgdp-1kg:{variant}:{label}', every row is healthy_reference with disease_ascertainment_excluded=True, and ac and an are stored as integer counts. That gives 77.73 rows per variant. 27,390 cells (0.34%) have an=0 or are missing; the contract requires an>0, so these are counted rather than written as rows. Validation used OBSERVATIONS_SCHEMA from the repo .venv. radius_km is a synthetic placeholder (no registry on disk); lat/lon are per-group means from the gnomAD HGDP+1KG sample metadata. A second window, chr2:100,000,001-101,000,000, gave 52,400 variants and 4,074,868 rows.

findings.claim: With DuckDB 1.5.5, zstd, rows sorted by (pos, ref, alt, population_id) and 122,880-row groups, a row with all 17 contract columns plus pos costs 2.465 B. source_record_id alone is 77% of that.
findings.evidence: Measured 2.465 B/row on chr21 and 2.452 on chr2. source_record_id is 1.843 B/row (stored PLAIN because every value is unique, about 41 characters). Every other column together is 0.545 B/row: an 0.145, ac 0.116, variant_id 0.087, rsid 0.081, pos 0.043, lat/lon/radius 0.049 together, population_id 0.017. DuckDB dictionary-encodes population_id automatically. source, assay, cohort_id, sampling_design, date_lower/upper and ingest_version are each 0.001 or less, and disease_ascertainment_excluded is about 0. So keeping the ascertainment fields on every row costs nothing. Without source_record_id the table is 0.621 B/row (chr2: 0.617). Writing source_record_id with prefix encoding (pyarrow, DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY) gives 1.150 B/row (chr2: 1.13).

findings.claim: Extrapolated to the whole genome (about 1.2e10 rows), the table is about 30 GB with source_record_id stored, about 14 GB with it prefix-encoded, and about 7.6 GB with it derived in the view. At 1e9 rows: about 2.5 GB, or 0.6 GB derived.
findings.evidence: Rows R = 153e6 variants x 80 populations = 1.224e10. The variant count is the published 'more than 153 million' (Koenig et al., Genome Research 34:796, 2024) and the design's own estimate. R is 1,534.8x the sample's rows. Sizes: 2.465 x 1.224e10 = 30.2 GB (28.1 GiB); 1.150 x R = 14.1 GB; 0.621 x R = 7.6 GB (7.1 GiB). Sample density is 51.3 variants per kb on chr21 and 52.4 on chr2; 153e6 over about 3.1 Gb is about 49 per kb, which is consistent. The assumption is that two windows represent the genome; they agree within 0.6% on bytes per row.

findings.claim: Four alternatives measured worse: 8,192-row groups (the design's §2.5 default), population-major order, keeping only rows with ac>0, and higher zstd or Parquet V2 settings.
findings.evidence: 8,192-row groups: 3.620 B/row (+47%, 44.3 GB at R). The footer is 1.05 MB per 1 Mb file against 70.7 KB at 122,880 rows. A one-variant lookup reads 1,070,172 B instead of 157,734 B, and a one-population scan needs 1,954 requests instead of 248. Population-major with all 17 columns: 15.25 B/row (186.7 GB), because variant_id, rsid and pos lose dictionary encoding and fall back to PLAIN. Only rows with ac>0: 8.855 B/row on 10.8% of rows, 11.7 GB. That is bigger than the derived-source_record_id layout (7.6 GB) and loses `an` for zero counts, which AGENTS.md calls weak evidence, not absence. zstd level 9: 2.485 B/row vs 2.465. Parquet V2: 2.643. Input order without sorting: 2.608.

findings.claim: Proposed layout: partition by chromosome and fixed 1 Mb position bins, with every bin file present, plus a narrow per-population copy for whole-genome scans of one population.
findings.evidence: Position table: tables/v1/measured/allele_observations/source=<s>/ingest_version=<iv>/chrom=<chrN>/bin=<floor(pos/1e6)>/part-0.parquet, sorted (pos, ref, alt, population_id), 122,880-row groups, with pos as an extra derived column. GRCh38 chr1-22, X and Y give 3,102 bins (chrM adds one), at about 4.0M rows per Mb. Each file is about 9.8 MB with source_record_id stored, or 2.5 MB derived: inside the design's 1-50 MB band. Ids with no locus (hla:, kir:, phenotype:) go under chrom=nonlocus. Gaps get a schema-only file so computed URLs never 404. Path values are checked against the data (bin == pos // 1e6, chromosome prefix of variant_id), since the probe files do not carry the partition columns. Population copy: measured/allele_counts_by_population/source=<s>/ingest_version=<iv>/population_id=<id>/chrom=<c>/part-0.parquet with columns pos, ref, alt, ac, an. Measured 2.567 B/row on chr21 and 1.955 on chr2, so 24-31 GB in 1,920 files. It holds counts only and stays under measured/, apart from surfaces. 5 Mb bins: 12-49 MB files and a 143.6 KB footer, so a one-variant lookup reads 246,999 B instead of 157,734.

findings.claim: On the 1 Mb-bin layout, one variant across all populations costs about 158 KB and 9-10 requests, and a gene costs about 1 MB and about 30 requests. Neither cost grows with genome size, as long as the query names the bin.
findings.evidence: Cold DuckDB 1.5.5 over the reused Range-logging server (scripts/rserve.py), with the HTTP metadata, external-file and Parquet metadata caches off. One variant (chr21-25950001-C-T): 157,734 B in 10 requests. The trace shows a HEAD, a 16 KB tail read, the 70,719 B footer, then that variant's row group. Over a 3,102-file genome-sized list (symlinks) with chrom and bin predicates: 244,837 B in 13 requests. DuckDB skips non-matching files by path but still opens the first listed file to read the schema. The APP gene (chr21:25,880,535-26,171,128, Ensembl GRCh38, spans 2 bins): 952,261 B in 28 requests; over the 3,102-file list 1,039,364 B in 31. With no partition predicate, every file is opened: 3,102 HEAD + 27,911 GET (31,013 requests). The symlinks repeat bin 25's data, so only that request count is meaningful there, not the bytes or rows.

findings.claim: One population across the whole genome reads about 4.9 GB in about 380,000 requests from the position table, but only about 0.3-0.45 GB from the per-population copy.
findings.evidence: Position table, measured on the sample: 3,215,068 B in 248 requests. Scaled by 1,534.8: 4.93 GB and 380,632 requests. Even returning only counts and sums it is 3.68 GB; with 1,048,576-row groups, 4.32 GB and 55,253 requests. Population copy: the sample query read 332,664 B in 5 requests. Scaling one population's sample file (288,980 B) by 153e6/102,594 = 1,491 gives 0.43 GB; chr2's density gives about 0.33 GB. A computed-URL macro read chr21 for one population in 83,197 B and 5 requests. The genome-scale request count for the copy (about 6,300) is a formula estimate, not measured: 24 files x 3 requests + (153e6/122,880) row groups x about 5 columns. The copy serves single-variant lookups badly: 24,067,594 B and 702 requests, because all 78 files open.

findings.claim: A design §3.1 catalog that lists every whole-genome file makes each attach about 5x heavier. Macros that build URLs from their arguments, which work in DuckDB 1.5.5, avoid this.
findings.evidence: atlas.duckdb with views over 3,102 + 1,920 URLs is 1,847,296 B, and a remote attach reads 2,895,876 B in 10 requests, against the 548,868 B the design measured. The local URLs used here are shorter than GCS ones, so the real file would be larger. A table macro whose read_parquet URL is built with string operations from the variant id reads 157,518 B in 9 requests and touches 1 file. Macros using list_transform(range(start//1e6, end//1e6+1), b -> base||...) for regions and list_transform(<24 chroms>, ...) for populations also work. The APP region via macro (counts and sums only) read 394,120 B in 28 requests.

findings.claim: What each query costs us from the bucket, and how many fit under the $300 kill switch.
findings.evidence: Prices: GCS regional Standard Class B is $0.0004 per 1,000 operations, and XML API GET Object and HEAD are both Class B. The free tier covers 50,000 Class B operations a month, us-east1/us-west1/us-central1 only. Egress is $0.12/GiB, as in the design. One variant: 0.000147 GiB x $0.12 + 10 ops = about $0.00002. A gene: about $0.0001. One population via the position table: 4.596 GiB x $0.12 + 380,632 x $0.0000004 = $0.70. Via the population copy: about $0.05. The kill switch (about 2,780 GB a month, design §8) allows about 563 position-table population scans, about 6,450 population-copy pulls, or about 17.6 million single-variant lookups a month.

findings.claim: Proposed threshold: anonymous DuckDB over HTTPS is the right path for any query that reads under about 1 GiB and about 10,000 requests. Anything that scans the position table genome-wide should go to a bulk download (from the mirror) plus local DuckDB, or to BigQuery with the querier paying.
findings.evidence: A genome-wide cross-population scan reads variant_id + population_id + ac + an, 0.365 B/row in position-major order, so 0.365 x 1.224e10 = about 4.5 GB and about 380,000 requests, like the population scan without the copy. At bandwidth alone that is 6.6 min at 100 Mbit/s and 0.7 min at 1 Gbit/s; the latency of 380,000 requests over a real network was not measured. The threshold matches OPEN_OBJECT_MAX_BYTES (1 GiB, about $0.12). By contrast the whole table is a one-off download: 7.1 GiB ($0.85 from GCS) derived, 28.1 GiB ($3.37) stored, and the population copy 29.3 GiB ($3.51). From a zero-egress mirror these cost us nothing.

findings.claim: The Hugging Face copy cannot be the query path; it suits only bulk downloads. And a whole-genome table in one release breaks the design's 2 GiB release guard unless a mirror carries it or the owner raises the cap.
findings.evidence: The design cites Hugging Face's limit of 3,000 anonymous requests per IP per 5 minutes [hf-rate]. A position-table scan needs about 380,000 requests and a population-copy pull about 6,300 (estimated). Single-variant and gene lookups (10-31 requests) would fit, but GCS already serves them for fractions of a cent. Size against the guard: the position table (7.6-30 GB) plus the population copy (24-31 GB) is about 32-61 GB per whole-genome ingest version, far over OPEN_RELEASE_GCS_MAX_BYTES (2 GiB of open bytes on no zero-egress host). It also adds about 5,000 objects per ingest version, which brings D14 (manifest over 2 MB) closer; that last point is estimated.

findings.claim: In a BigQuery copy of the whole-genome table, storage billed on logical bytes would cost us about $47-68 a month, far above the design's 'about $0.92'. Physical (compressed) billing probably brings it to about $1. Scans stay cheap for the querier.
findings.evidence: BigQuery sizes: STRING = 2 + UTF-8 bytes, INT64/FLOAT64 = 8, BOOL = 1, NULL = 0. From sample string lengths that is 257.7 logical B/row (source_record_id 43.1, ingest_version 41.0, variant_id 20.8). Times R: 3.15 TB = 2.87 TiB. Monthly storage (hourly page rate x 730 h; the page's default location view, not confirmed as the US multi-region): 2,938 GiB x $0.000031507 = $68 active logical; x $0.000021918 = $47 long-term logical. Physical billing is a per-dataset choice; time travel (at least 2 days) is then billed separately. If BigQuery compresses like Parquet (not measured), that is 7-28 GiB x $0.000054795 x 730 = $0.28-1.12. Queries: a cross-population scan bills 49.4 B x R = 0.55 TiB, which fits once a month in the querier's free TiB, then costs $3.44 at $6.25/TiB. One population, assuming clustering on population_id prunes as expected, is about 7.6 GB, so about 145 fit in the free TiB. Minimum 10 MB per table referenced.

findings.claim: Building the whole-genome table means streaming the full 3.63 TB genotype callset. The per-population INFO fields cannot be used, because they merge 80 populations into 78.
findings.evidence: The callset's INFO has exactly 78 AC_<group> fields (measured). The repo's count pilot (docs/research/hgdp-count-pilot-2026-09-09.md) found Han/NorthernHan and PapuanHighlands/PapuanSepik merged under single labels, and the gnomAD metadata 'population' field also yields 78 groups. A raw harvest built from INFO would therefore merge 4 identities into 2 without any error from the adapter. HEAD sizes of the 24 per-chromosome VCFs sum to 3,631,210,123,548 B (chr2 alone 295,199,118,882 B). At the 27.7 MB/s single-stream download measured here, that is about 36 hours (estimate). A free GitHub runner's 14 GB disk forces streaming. This is offline batch work, never the serving path.

findings.claim: Whether to store or derive source_record_id is a contract decision that has to be made before step 1.2 freezes the contracts. It is the single largest size lever.
findings.evidence: Stored as DuckDB writes it: 30.2 GB. Prefix-encoded (pyarrow writer, which breaks builder's call 15, 'one pinned DuckDB writes every file'): 14.1 GB. Derived in the catalog view as 'gnomad-hgdp-1kg:' || variant_id || ':' || <source label>, keeping the source label as a cheap dictionary column and recording the formula in measured.ingests: 7.6 GB. The derived form returns the same 17 columns: a lookup read 160,146 B in 9 requests vs 157,734 B in 10 stored. Integrity check 4 (re-ingest gives the same source_record_id set) still holds if the check recomputes the formula. For sources whose ids are not derivable (literature, MAP), source_record_id stays stored.

research: layout.implications:
Owner question first: before step 1.2 freezes the v1 contracts, decide whether the whole-genome table stores `source_record_id` or derives it in the view. It is the biggest size lever: 30.2 GB stored, 14.1 GB prefix-encoded, or 7.6 GB derived.

A whole-genome observations layer does not need a warehouse for the three common queries, as long as the layout is right. The design's D4 line ("1.2e10 rows need a warehouse") overstates it.

**Recommended layout**
- Path: `tables/v1/measured/allele_observations/source=<s>/ingest_version=<iv>/chrom=<chrN>/bin=<floor(pos/1e6)>/part-0.parquet`.
- Sort rows by (pos, ref, alt, population_id).
- Use 122,880-row groups, overriding §2.5's 8,192 for this table: 8,192 is 47% larger and reads 7x more for a one-variant lookup.
- Add `pos` as an extra derived column, put ids with no locus (hla:, kir:, phenotype:) under `chrom=nonlocus`, and write every bin file, empty ones included.
- Add a narrow count-only copy, `measured/allele_counts_by_population/.../population_id=<id>/chrom=<c>/`, holding pos, ref, alt, ac and an (24-31 GB). It stays under measured/, apart from surfaces.
- Counts stay as ac and an. Keeping only rows with ac>0 is rejected: it is no smaller than deriving `source_record_id`, and it loses `an` for zero counts.

**Expected query costs on that layout**
- One variant across all populations: about 158 KB and 9-10 requests.
- A gene (APP): about 1 MB and about 30 requests.
- One population genome-wide: about 0.3-0.45 GB from the narrow copy, against about 4.9 GB and about 380,000 requests from the position table.

**Catalog (§2.6)**
- Ship macros that build URLs from their arguments: variant, region and population. They work in DuckDB 1.5.5.
- Listing all 5,000 or so URLs in `atlas.duckdb` makes every attach about 2.9 MB.

**Where anonymous HTTPS stops**
- A query that would read the position table genome-wide (about 4.5 GB and 380,000 requests, about $0.70 to us each) goes elsewhere.
- One option is a bulk download of the table (7-61 GB, free to us from a zero-egress mirror) queried locally.
- The other is BigQuery with the querier paying: a cross-population scan bills 0.55 TiB. Its dataset should use physical storage billing, because logical billing would cost us about $47-68 a month.

**D3 re-ask, reframed for query-first**
- The free Hugging Face copy cannot serve queries: its anonymous limit (3,000 requests per 5 minutes) is far below what scans need.
- The mirror is still needed for bulk downloads and for the release guard: a whole-genome ingest of 32-61 GB breaks the 2 GiB guard unless a mirror carries it or the owner raises the cap.

**`fetch_data.py` filters map onto partitions:** `--table` with a chromosome or population filter selects files by path.

**Build-side requirement:** correct 80-population counts must come from the 3.63 TB genotype callset, streamed offline; the INFO fields merge them into 78 groups.

**What is measured and what is not**
- Measured: bytes per row on two real gnomAD windows (chr21 and chr2), and request counts on a local server.
- Extrapolated by arithmetic: everything at genome scale.
- Not measured: network latency, and how BigQuery compresses the table.

All scripts and results are under <scratchpad>/wg/obs-layout/ (`scripts/`, `out/*.json`, `out/extrapolation.txt`).

Recount the v3.1.2 HGDP + 1KG genotypes (CC0) for the paper's 4,094 people under all 80 identities, by **D18's rule, in full** (below the table). It replaces "the chr22 pilot's rules", which covered only PASS biallelic SNVs on an autosome. `cohort_id` names the release, sample stage and rule. Relatedness (1,294 reported pairs in the pilot) is left to the fitting side, never pruned from the measurement.

D18's rule, in full (what approving D18 approves; nothing in it is inherited by reference):
1. Input and stage. gnomAD v3.1.2's HGDP + 1KG dense VCFs: 24 files, chr1–22, X and Y; there is no chrM file. Samples: the paper's 4,094 (the stage is a parameter, named in `cohort_id`). Each sample's population is the source's literal population field, 80 identities, read from the metadata file recorded by sha256 (D17).
2. Records. FILTER = PASS; every other record is counted per filter in `measured.ingests`, not ingested. The callset is already split, one ALT per record (measured: none of 11,374 records in five windows has a second ALT; 22 of 583 and 198 of 3,437 positions in the chr22 and chr11 windows carry two or more records). A record with a second ALT or a `*` ALT, or a genotype allele index above 1, fails the build. Every ALT is its own `chr-pos-ref-alt` row: SNVs, indels and MNPs alike (12–15% of records are not SNVs: 72 of 616 and 560 of 3,812 in two windows). The pilot's PASS-biallelic-SNV selection was the pilot's scope, not part of this rule, and its hand controls do not yet cover indels (step 2.6 adds them).
3. Calls. A call counts if GQ ≥ 20, DP ≥ 10 (DP ≥ 5 for a haploid call, gnomAD's own default thresholds, [gnomad-adj]) and, if heterozygous, each of its two AD values divided by DP ≥ 0.2. A failing or missing call lowers `an` and never becomes a reference call; refusals are counted per population and reason (missing, low GQ, low DP, low allele balance, in that order). A partial genotype such as `./1` fails the build.
4. Sex chromosomes. Ploidy follows gnomAD's `gnomad_sex_imputation.sex_karyotype`, the authority. The stage holds only XX and XY samples: all 30 others in the callset (20 X, 2 XXY, 2 XYY, 6 ambiguous) are gnomAD hard-filtered (`sex_aneuploidy`, `ambiguous_sex`), and a stage that keeps any fails the build for you to decide. The pseudoautosomal regions (PARs), as the callset's Hail 0.2.77 GRCh38 reference defines them ([hail-grch38]): chrX:10,001–2,781,479 and chrX:155,701,383–156,030,895, diploid for everyone. chrX outside the PARs: XX diploid; XY haploid, adding 1 to `an` and 0 or 1 to `ac`, never 2. chrY outside the PARs: XY haploid; XX samples are not in the denominator. chrY's PARs (chrY:10,001–2,781,479 and 56,887,903–57,217,415) hold no records (measured): their variation is called on chrX. A called genotype whose ploidy differs from this fails the build.
5. Sites and cells. A PASS record is written if its recounted `ac` is above 0 in the stage; one with no allele in the stage is counted (`monomorphic_in_stage`), not written. Every population at a written record is a row, ac = 0 included, unless its `an` is 0 (counted per population, not written; builder's call 32).
6. Scope. chrX and chrY ship in v1 under items 4 and 5.

Measured on 2026-10-19 (`wg/apply-checks/`; a 4,097-sample stand-in stage, gnomAD's `high_quality` samples, with the sample-meta file's 78 labels): every called genotype's ploidy matched item 4 in two chrX PAR windows, a chrX non-PAR window (XY: 8,195,765 haploid calls, 0 diploid) and a chrY window (XX: all missing); the native bcftools count and an independent Python counter agreed on all 592,484 written cells of the chr11 (rs334), chrX non-PAR and chrY windows; DP ≥ 5 rather than 10 keeps 262,267 of 8,141,719 XY chrX calls (3.2%) and 19,185 of 1,199,713 chrY calls (1.6%); PASS records with no allele in the stage were 2.1% (chr11), 5.9% (chrX) and 3.0% (chrY).
